standard_prerequisites.name: Enumerable set
standard_prerequisites.statement: A set A is enumerable when there is a surjection from the positive integers onto A, or equivalently when its members can be listed.
standard_prerequisites.use: The proof starts from an arbitrary listing of a subset of the binary sequences and derives a sequence missing from the list (source lines 1176-1180).

standard_prerequisites.name: Infinite binary strings
standard_prerequisites.statement: The set of infinite sequences of 0s and 1s, written as the set of functions from the natural numbers to the two symbols.
standard_prerequisites.use: The array of digits and the constructed string d are both infinite binary strings (source lines 1176-1200).

core_obligations: Set up the double indexing: given a list s_0, s_1, ... of binary sequences, read it as an array in which s_n(m) sits at row n and column m, and display the array (source lines 1176-1190).
Define the diagonal string d by d(n) = 1 if s_n(n) = 0 and d(n) = 0 if s_n(n) = 1, so that d differs from the diagonal of the array at every coordinate (source lines 1191-1204).

Show that d appears in no row of the list: for a fixed n compare d with s_n and conclude, by the two cases of the definition of d(n), that d(n) is different from s_n(n), so d is not equal to any s_n and the set of binary sequences admits no enumeration (source lines 1205-1222).

proof_roadmap.step: Read an arbitrary enumeration as an infinite array of digits.
Define the diagonal string d by flipping every diagonal entry.
For each n show d differs from s_n at coordinate n, so no enumeration lists every binary sequence.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own theorem at source lines 1170-1173: the set of infinite binary sequences is not enumerable. The proof at source lines 1175-1222 is Cantor's diagonal argument carried out in full, and it is not a one-step application of a previously stated theorem in the unit. It has to set up the double indexing of an arbitrary enumeration as an infinite array of digits, define the diagonal string by flipping the diagonal entries, and then show by a genuine case analysis that the resulting string agrees with no row of the array: for a fixed row n the two strings differ at coordinate n, and the definition of d(n) makes that difference explicit in each of the two cases. The proof also has to be careful about the direction of the enumeration hypothesis, since it argues against an enumeration of a subset of the binary sequences rather than of the whole set. No result outside the retained text is used.
